items.followUp: Define one mole and give an example of one mole of oxygen molecules.

rubric.why: A mole is defined by the number of elementary entities it contains.
rubric.description: States that one mole contains Avogadro’s number of entities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the number of entities in a mole.

rubric.why: An example demonstrates the amount of substance represented by a mole.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of one mole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as 1 mol of carbon atoms.

modelAnswer: A mole is the amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, etc.).
For example, 1 mol of carbon contains 6.02 × 10²³ carbon atoms.

items.followUp: Write the subshell electronic configuration of the oxide ion, O²⁻.

rubric.why: The first ten electrons fill the 1s, 2s and 2p subshells.
Chloride has 18 electrons, so the third shell is filled through 3p⁶.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for adding 3s² 3p⁶ to the configuration.

modelAnswer: A chlorine atom gains one electron to form Cl⁻, giving it 18 electrons.
The subshell electronic configuration of Cl⁻ is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶.

items.followUp: State two observations from Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles travelled through the foil without significant deflection.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed through the foil undeflected or nearly undeflected.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the observation about most particles passing straight through.

rubric.why: A small number of alpha particles were deflected at large angles or returned.
rubric.description: States that some particles were deflected or a very few bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either observation about deflection or backscattering.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed through the gold foil without being deflected.
Some alpha particles were deflected, and a very few bounced back.

items.followUp: Describe how metallic character changes across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: Electronegativity generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.description: Gives the trend across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electronegativity increases across a period.

rubric.why: Electronegativity generally decreases down a group.
rubric.description: Gives the trend down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electronegativity decreases down a group.

modelAnswer: Across a period, electronegativity generally increases from left to right.
Down a group, electronegativity generally decreases from top to bottom.

items.followUp: What is meant by atomic radius, and name a commonly used unit for it.

rubric.why: Atomic radius describes the size of an atom as a distance from its nucleus or by half the internuclear distance of identical bonded atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of atomic radius.

rubric.why: Atomic radii are commonly expressed in picometres or angstroms.
rubric.description: Gives a valid unit for atomic radius.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for pm, picometre, or angstrom.

modelAnswer: Atomic radius is the distance from the centre of an atom’s nucleus to its outermost electron shell.
It is commonly measured in picometres (pm).

items.followUp: How do elements in the same group differ from elements in the same period in the periodic table?

rubric.why: Periods and groups are distinguished by their orientation in the periodic table.
rubric.description: Identifies periods as horizontal rows and groups as vertical columns.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly distinguishing the orientation of periods and groups.

rubric.why: The elements’ shell or valence-electron relationships further distinguish periods from groups.
rubric.description: Gives a correct characteristic distinguishing elements in a period from those in a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that period members have the same number of occupied shells, or group members have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties.

modelAnswer: Periods are horizontal rows, whereas groups are vertical columns in the periodic table.
Elements in the same period have the same number of occupied electron shells; elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties.

items.followUp: Write any two physical properties of covalent compounds.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds commonly have strong electrostatic attractions and form crystalline, hard, brittle solids with high melting points.
rubric.description: States one valid physical property of ionic compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct property, such as high melting point or crystalline, hard and brittle nature.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds conduct when their ions are mobile and many dissolve in water.
rubric.description: States a second valid physical property of ionic compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another correct property, such as electrical conductivity when molten or dissolved in water, or solubility in water.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.

items.followUp: Write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of calcium with oxygen and nitrogen.

rubric.why: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide; the equation must be balanced.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced reaction of magnesium with oxygen.

rubric.why: Magnesium reacts with nitrogen to form magnesium nitride; the equation must be balanced.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced reaction of magnesium with nitrogen.
